job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in software engineering in Kumasi and I live in the university's postgraduate hostel. I wake at six, pray, then code until lunch with an AI assistant doing the boring parts. In the afternoon I teach a free coding class to teenagers at my church, and in the evening I call my mother in Techiman. Last summer I interned at a payments start-up in Accra, where I fixed bugs in a mobile-money app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is useful but overhyped, and hard work still matters most. At church I'd say God gives gifts and we use tools wisely. Online I'd say building things matters more than posting about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me a plateau is fine. Software is still needed, mobile money is growing and I have a good record. I use AI tools every day, but they help me work faster, they don't do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a job at the payments start-up or a bank, and keep teaching teenagers on Saturdays. I'd send money to my mother each month, about a fifth of my pay. I'd try to build a small app on the side that helps market traders track their stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, steady. Not exciting, but I don't need it to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the app for market traders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt sells tomatoes at Techiman market and writes everything in a paper notebook. She loses money when prices change or when she forgets who owes her. A simple phone app with voice notes could solve that, and I'd charge a few cedis a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries in the plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother's school fees, mostly. My parents rely on me a bit. If my first salary is delayed by two months, we feel it. That's the pressure I carry, with or without AI.

At church I'd say God gives gifts and we use **tools wisely**.
think: A plateau is fine because software is still needed and **mobile money** is growing.
AI tools make me **faster**, but they don't do the work for me.
do: Finish the master's and take a job at the **payments start-up** or a bank.
Send a fifth of my pay to my **mother** and build a stock app for market traders.
feel: I feel **steady**, not exciting, but I don't need it to be.

Send a fifth of my pay to my mother each month
Build a voice-note stock app for market traders like my aunt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but a big chance. I'd tell my class and my church teens to learn to build with these tools now, because the people who use them will lead. I'd tell friends not to wait for the government to hand out answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of junior coding work goes to the tools, which includes the kind of jobs I'm aiming for. But I'm already working with them every day, and in Ghana there's a huge need for software that fits local life. I'm not safe, but I'm early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the market app within six months and try to get two hundred traders on it. I'd apply to three payments and fintech firms and ask my internship manager for a reference. I'd also expand the church coding class to adults, because there's demand and it earns a small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a door opening, and I'm one of the first ones near it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a classmate who doesn't use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come to my desk for an hour and watch. I'm not showing off, it's like teaching someone to ride a bike. Once they see that it speeds up their own work, the fear drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's most at risk around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The call-centre workers and data-entry clerks, many of whom are young women with families. Those jobs are the first ones software eats. I'd want my church to start a small fund or a training class for them.

Start a church training fund for call-centre workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a hurricane, but I'd still say start building. I'd tell my class to launch things this year and not wait for jobs. At church I'd say we pray, but we also prepare, and I'd start a savings group for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. By 2028 the junior developer jobs I'm preparing for would mostly be gone, and my family counts on my income. I'd be 26, with a brother in school and a mother who can't rely on me being unemployed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's early if a fintech offers me a job, because the first salary is worth more than the second degree. I'd launch the market app now and aim for a thousand traders, which is the only product I know has a real need. I'd also help my mother set up a mobile-money wallet and a small savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy. I carry my family on my back, and I'm choosing to be strong about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay his school fees first, before anything else, even before rent. He's fifteen and bright, and I'd rather live in a smaller room than let my brother's school stop. That's my promise to our mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to cut taxes on small firms and let people start businesses quickly. Handouts help in a crisis, but a market trader with a working app needs a licence, not a cheque.

I'd start a **savings group** for families at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build something, so I'd tell friends to do so. I'd tell the church we need to train young people in practical skills like coding, repairs and bookkeeping. I'd say the economy will reward people who make things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay. By 2031 I'd have three years of work and maybe a small company, which helps against the thinking tasks going to AI. The hands-on robots come around 2034, but they'd reach Ghana later because of cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for a fintech for two years, learn how money systems run, and then start my own company for market traders and small shops. I'd keep sending money home, and I'd save for a plot of land in Kumasi. I'd marry my fiancée Abena in 2030 if our savings permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, with a sprinkle of fear. The good kind of fear, like before a match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra years change compared to two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to learn on someone else's budget, and that matters. With two years I'd be forced to start before I'm ready. With five I can learn how a payments firm survives, then do it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your company failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to a salaried job with no shame. A failed company is a story you tell at dinner, not a stain. My pastor says the same, and he has failed twice.

I'd say the economy will reward people who **make things**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift. I'd tell everyone to plan carefully, start small businesses and pay attention to what skills matter. I'd say churches should build training centres, because they already have the people and the trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 34, probably running a company with twenty staff and supporting my family comfortably. The hands-on robots around 2039 are a long way off in Ghana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the company slowly, hire local graduates and train them on the job. I'd use AI tools to make my small team do more, and I'd keep teaching. I'd also invest in a small farm in Techiman for my parents, which feels like a sensible way to spread risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm and ambitious. I'd be working hard, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a training centre next to our church with free evening classes in coding and bookkeeping. I'd fund it with part of the company's profit. People who get a start tend to give the next person one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who thinks it's all a bubble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say maybe, but even if it is, the skills still stand. A person who can build and sell software can adapt to the next thing. I'd rather be ready for nothing than unready for something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my family depends on me and I would have no time to build a track record. What would help is simple business licences, cheap internet and a loan scheme for young founders. I'd also want banks to hire local graduates rather than import talent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people think Africa will be left out. I think we could be early on the things that matter here, like mobile money and markets. I'd like someone to build for that, and I'd like to be the one.

headlineQuote: Handouts help in a crisis, but a market trader with a working app needs a licence, not a cheque.
portrait: Umar is 24, doing a **software engineering** master's in Kumasi, using AI tools every day and teaching a church coding class.
His traditional, free-market outlook favours **business**, family duty and community training over handouts.
His family depends on his income, and he pays attention to his brother's school fees.
He sees AI as a **chance** to build locally, such as an app for market traders like his aunt.
In the fast scenario he becomes anxious but chooses to **launch and earn** early.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his family depends on him and there would be no time to build a track record.
whatWouldHelp: Simple **business licences**, cheap internet and a loan scheme for young founders.
